I've been playing vidya a long fucking time, and have a couple experiences that have stayed with me my entire life.

Metroid

This was one of the defining moments of my life as a gamer. It was Christmas Eve, 1986 I believe, the year that Nintendo was the big thing and you could buy the big box set with the gun and the little robot. My second cousin (in his 20s) got that box for Christmas and my father and I went to his place (just across the street from where our family Christmas Eve party was happening, to check it out. I was 5 or 6.

Metroid was the game my cousin was showing off. I'd played Atari and Colecovision games before and thought I knew about games, but it blew my mind when he RAN TO THE LEFT to get the morphball. Waaaaaat? I was impressed by this deviation from what I considered the norm but what got me, and permanently affected me, was what happened next.

I noticed there was no score.

"Where is the score?" I asked my cousin.

"There is no score," he replied. "You just have to get to the end."

And that was it, that was all it took to shatter my preconceptions of videogames, for my small child's brain to make the leap from 'videogames are games' to 'videogames are ADVENTURES.' It was such a paradigm shift for me that it literally changed my life and I will never forget it, it was a perfect moment for a gamer to have.

Ultima Underworld: The Stygian Abyss

I could go on forever about this game but let's just say it established expectations for the genre of firsperson-RPGs that has never since been exceeded. Even the best dungeon crawlers and FPRPGs fall short of the highwater mark UU set way back in 1994. A spiritual successor by some of the original devs is currently in development and I have high hopes for it indeed.

Fallout 1

I played Fallout 1 when it was still new, bought the weird oblong box with the flip-up cover and everything (on sale for like 10 bucks a couple months after release). I'd read it was the RPG of the year but the beginning of the game (stabbing rats for 15 minutes) was underwhelming and I gave up. I tried it again a couple days later, committed to winning, and I got into the game proper, which was, well, you probably know, amazing.

The lasting impression was two fold: first, Fallout was the first (and is still one of the only) games where your intelligence score effects conversation options, which meant traditional min-maxing was pointless. Second, I beat the game but totally bypassed the final boss, because my character was a thief and snuck into the basement of the last area, armed a nuclear bomb, and escaped. I didn't even KNOW there was a final boss until a friend asked me about it weeks later. I've never played a game since that let me do that.

Halflife

I played Halflife before it released; the 'OEM' version was included with certain videocards allowing you to play right up to, I believe, the Surface Tension chapter. My friend had acquired it and, well, it was college so we did a bunch of acid and proceeded to check the game out. We could tell from the training that the game was awesome but what happened next is what I will never forget.

We started up the game proper and were on the monorail. I sat back, lit a cigarette, and we watched as the monorail did its thing. Maybe a minute into the sequence I went to flick my cigarette, accidentally hit the mouse and... HOLY SHIT THE SCREEN MOVED.

And we realized, we were ON the fucking monorail. We could walk around, look around, focus on whatever. It can not be overstated how amazing this was to us at the time, not because of the drugs (though they helped) but because this was the first time anything like this ever happened in a game. The entire introductory sequence with Freeman going to work... it was amazing, there was nothing like it, and it changed my expectations of videogames forever.

Homeworld

The first game that made me cry. The ending was just so beautiful.

I could go on and on and on, I have been affected by so many games, but this is long enough I think, ha.

Metroid. I can not agree with that more than any other game. You really kinda need to be an oldfag to understand. You have to understand what was possible in other games AT THAT TIME. Based on that, your first time playing Metroid was always going to be mind-blowing. It was amazing. It was a time when games could come along and totally shake up game play in general. Metroid did that for me. Thanks for mentioning it first.

No problem, friend, it is probably my favorite story to share with oldschool gamers because they understand. I could have had a similar experience with Legend of Zelda, I suppose, but even that would have been different because there is something much more... visceral, I suppose, about a sidescroller, and also the mechanics of sidescrollers were something my child's mind thought it understood. Metroid changed all that, it implied this crazy narrative that was going on that was just so much richer than anything else I'd ever encountered, and despite the power of that initial revelatory experience it was really only the first of many as I came to learn its ways: the secret energy tank in the first area, the way you could face the bosses way too early, the nonlinear weapon and item progression, the menacing quality of the enemies and the sheer variety of monsters you face... Metroid changed my life and changed what I thought videogames could achieve. I still remember using graph paper to make Metroid-like games and levels for those games... in 2nd grade.

Many people did not encounter Metroid again until the SNES masterpiece Super Metroid but I was fortunate, I saved all my birthday money in 1991 and bought myself a Gameboy. That winter, Metroid 2 came out for Gameboy and, well, honestly, I fucking hated it at first. I just didn't grasp the gameplay. And it was hard as hell. But somehow eventually I got the ball rolling (you need to kill a certain number of weird Metroid hybrids to unlock further areas while also getting powerups) and came to realize that Metroid 2 is just as good as the first, and did a wonderful job expanding Samus's arsenal. And Super Metroid, of course, requires no comment, though I will say I did not have a SNES so it was years before I got to play it through. Regardless, the experience was amazingly powerful, especially as it actually continues the Metroid 2 story line (that it feels like no one but me played).

Anyway, I'm rambling as I wait to get out of work, but I'm really glad I'm not alone with having such a powerful early gaming experience with Metroid. I don't understand why the Japanese weren't more into the series, by all accounts it is simply no where near as popular there as here.

It might be cliche but Majora's Mask really affected me. First off, the game is just so different from other Zelda games and I think it really gave the player a genuine feeling of looming doom. Most games try that, but you don't ever really get that feeling in my opinion. Secondly, I played that game when it first came out and I could not for the life of me figure out how to get out of the deku scrub form for quite some time. As a result, I watched the end of the world cutscene many times. Each time, I was just as scared. Although I was a stupid 10 year old, I think it was intentionally designed to have you fail at least once at the beginning so you could see that horrific cutscene and really understand what you're up against.

What resonated with me overall however, was the role of cause and effect in the game. Everything in that game that you do--or don't--do has an effect that you can actually see later on. It really led to me caring about the characters even if they were NPCs that acted according to a timing system. Even now when I play the game I get this heavy feeling that I have to do everything in the first 3-day cycle because I feel bad if I do not. However, it is also pretty much impossible so it forces you to choose what you want to do. I end up telling myself that I'll just turn back time and reset everything, but for some reason that is not as comforting as you might think. By showing you the consequences of actions and then getting the chance to reset and do things differently Majora's Mask taught me a lot about empathy. It helped shape my mind and think in the long term when I see someone asking/needing help and how the situation looks from their perspective.

I'm not well versed in higher-level philosophy and logic terms so forgive me if I step on any toes. I mostly wanted feedback on an issue I've been debating with myself, especially with the "fattening" causing such uproar. I am a staunch proponent of free speech(This talk by Hitchens gives a good idea of my mentality) but that being said I wish for a society of acceptance and peace. I absolutely abhor tribalism and contend that things that engender a tribal mentality are general bad for the world. My mental clash appears in issues like the restaurant refusing to serve homosexuals recently. It is a privately owned restaurant. I feel that government shouldn't ever step in if a place refuses to serve whites/gays/black/etc. That stance goes so far as to say that the requirements for businesses to have wheelchair access crosses a line. I know very well that a lack of such requirements will likely lead to businesses catering to specific subsets of people...which would encourage tribalism. My question is if anyone has explored this issue before and has found a way to countenance supporting hardline free-speech while not becoming increasingly concerned with a rise in tribalism.

Note: I am fine with government operated organizations being required to enforce equality, my qualm is specifically with private business and even private actions of free speech (hate speech being an example)
